psy-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone II: Experimental Research Design in Psychology and Interdisciplinary Case Conceptualization
explain: The final task of the bachelor's course in psychology is to select one specific psychological phenomenon or problem situation and to carry out **(1) a multilevel case conceptualization from biological, cognitive, developmental/personality, and social psychological perspectives**, and **(2) write a rigorous experimental research design proposal to test or improve it**. Keep in mind that this task is training in academic research design and theoretical conceptualization, not an actual clinical diagnosis or treatment prescription.

A complete psychology capstone report consists of five parts. First, **[Defining the phenomenon and operational definitions]**: select the psychological construct to be explored (for example, memory decline due to smartphone multitasking, social isolation, test anxiety, or bystander behavior) and give it an **operational definition** in concrete indicators that can be observed and measured (for example, reaction time in ms, number of words recalled, or a T-score scale).

Second, **[Multilevel theoretical model and case conceptualization]**: link why the phenomenon arises and persists to theories from at least three subfields of psychology. For example, organically combine Baddeley's **working memory model** or **prospect theory** (cognitive), the **amygdala, autonomic nervous system, and neurotransmitters** (biological), **the attachment internal working model and Big Five traits** (developmental and personality), **attribution biases, cognitive dissonance, and social influence** (social), and the **diathesis-stress model and negative reinforcement** (abnormal and clinical).

Third, **[Experimental design and control of extraneous variables]**: specify the **independent variable (manipulated) and dependent variable (measured)** for testing the hypothesis, build a $2 \times 2$ **factorial design**, and describe the expected **main effects and interaction effect**. Here, state concretely how you would apply **random assignment**, a placebo control group, and the **double-blind procedure** in a between-subjects design, or **counterbalancing** in a within-subjects design, to block threats to internal validity (selection bias, order effects, regression to the mean, and so on).

Fourth, **[Psychometric and statistical testing plan]**: present how to secure the **reliability** (internal consistency and so on) and **validity** (construct validity and so on) of the instruments that measure the dependent variable, and specify the criteria for interpreting not only the simple $p$-value but also the **effect size** and standard scores ($Z, T$). Fifth, **[Research ethics and limits of external validity]**: honestly reflect on principles of research ethics such as informed consent, debriefing, and confidentiality, and on the limits of generalizing experimental results to the real world.

examples.title: Example of an integrated experimental research proposal: the effect of anxiety level (personality) × cognitive restructuring treatment (CBT) on working memory performance
body: 1. Operational definitions: trait anxiety scale T score of 60 or above (high anxiety) vs. 45 or below (low anxiety); treatment is 15 minutes of cognitive restructuring training vs. a simple reading control; the dependent variable is backward digit span (working memory span).

2. 2×2 factorial design hypothesis: because cognitive restructuring training reduces catastrophizing thoughts and restores central executive capacity only in the high-anxiety group, the gain in working memory score will be much larger than in the low-anxiety group (interaction effect).

3. Control design: within each anxiety level, participants are randomly assigned to the training group and the control group, and the test administrator applies a blind procedure in which he or she does not know the participant's group.

examples.title: Four-point core checklist for research ethics
body: 1. Voluntary participation and informed consent (one may stop at any time without penalty). 2. Minimizing physical and psychological harm. 3. When unavoidable deception is used, restoring the participant to the prior state through immediate debriefing right after the experiment. 4. Anonymity and confidentiality of personal information and data.
